doc.title: Jon Hendricks interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 29, 2000 [interview 2 of 2]

title: Hearing Salt Peanuts on the ship and buying bebop records
summary: Heard Bird and Diz on the troopship radio, bought every bebop record, and turned Toledo musicians on.

story.theme_name: Charlie Parker, Dizzy and the bebop revolution
story.community_name: Charlie Parker: encounters, lore and legacy

blocks.x: Detroit and seeing Diz and Charlie Parker there. And didn’t Charlie Parker tell you to pursue music or something like that? © Hamilton College Jazz Archive -11-
Well we had this bandstand conversation. I think we covered this in our last interview but I’ll go over it again.

We had this quick bandstand conversation. I had all his records when I came out of the Army. I had heard “Salt Peanuts” on the ship. I had won $300 shooting craps on the boat, and I heard this record from the ship’s radio room [scats]. I said whoa. Because it was in my head already from my Art Tatum days. And you know I heard Art Tatum, so I ran up to the radio room and I said to the guy, “what’s that record you just played?” Because by that time he’s playing something else. He said, “I don’t know it’s down there on the floor.” And I looked down and the floor’s covered with records. I says, “what kind of a label was it?” He says, “it had a red label.” So I looked down there and finally I found this Musicraft red label thing called “Salt Peanuts.” I says, “hey, is this it?” And he was talking on the radio, and then he says, “yeah, that’s it — Salt Peanuts, with Dizzy Gillespie and Charlie Parker.” So I gave him 25 bucks and I said, “play this for the next hour.” And so he played this record — drove everybody crazy on the ship. People came up to the radio, “what the hell is that? Play something else?”
Forget it, man, I’ve got 25 bucks.

But I couldn’t believe that and so I says whoa, man. So when I landed in Baltimore I immediately went to the nearest record shop and the guy told me where I could find Bird and Diz’s records. Because they weren’t sold in the respectable music shops. You had to go to the little dedicated jazz people to buy these records. So I bought as many of them as I could get my hands on and I bought anything that had to do with bebop, and bought Dave Lambert and Buddy Stewart. Because at that time in the store you could go in a little booth and you could play the records to see if you wanted to buy them. And I bought everything I could get my hands on that had to do with bebop. I had a whole cardboard box full of these 78s. Because when I heard that I heard what I had heard when I was 14, 15 with Art Tatum. You know I worked with him for two years at the Waiter’s & Bellman’s Club. And Art was the father of bebop — you know the chord substitutions and the speed with which he played, and the tempo changes. Especially the advanced harmonics — the 9th and 13th chords. I had heard all that then. So by the time I got to Toledo, I was the only cat into that. Everybody was where we had left off, you know, Lunceford, Basie, Ellington, they were still there. But I was into this — they said, “what is this stuff?” And I turned a lot of musicians in Toledo on to Bebop, as I’d invite them over to listen to my records.
